In response to 15:56 I don't think this may be much of an issue, in theory.

For one, if companies have a robust enough ranked match-making system, then in the least you would be playing against AI bots at your level. Not ideal if you want to play against only human players, but they won't necessarily will be dominating.

And two, verification could exist in many forms to help mitigate it. In the least ID verification of some form, that if it is found out you were using an AI, you would be banned and it would be known and shared to other gaming companies. Sort of like a human gaming credit score. But there are a multitude of ways to mitigate this. In the least maybe IRL LAN parties and gaming cafes make a resurgence again.

And three, honestly, at least in my opinion, if I am having just as much fun (if not more) playing with AI agents/bots, then it really isn't an issue. Least for me personally. Sort of a cop out point, but sometimes a really toxic human player can ruin a game as well.

comments.text:
I was struck by a thought as Wes explained that SIMA has a virtual keyboard and mouse: I'm worried that goal-oriented agentic AI is a lot scarier in terms of leading to problematic scenarios like the "paper clip scenario" vs. LLMs.

 From the little bit that I've played around with ML, I know that reward algorithms are everything. With ChatGPT RLHF, the reward algo is basically a human judging whether the output is helpful and accurate. For agents, I think the reward algo is much more centered around goal achievement. I could imagine that if a game-playing agent develops language skills in the process of training to accomplish tasks, then it will be wielding language as a tool to accomplish goals, potentially leading it to be very manipulative.

I suppose it's possible to include helpfulness (and, by proxy, friendliness) in the training algo as well to help ensure that achieving goals only gets a positive reward when the result was helpful to humans rather than hurtful. But then you start getting into all the crazy scenarios that AI scientists and science fiction worry about like the trolly problem.

I do think that AI mapping work like the project from Anthropic could potentially help a ton. It may be able to do things like showing humans when an AI is being deceptive, etc.

comments.text:
From an evolutionary POV, it would make sense that brains are complex, adapted collections of interactions that happened to produce good results. Good defined as survived well enough to have progeny that had progeny.
If simple weighted networks were useful then networks with more weights and deeper layers, if properly addapted and culled, would produce better results, until they don't.
From this POV, feeding a nascent set of weigted deep neural nets interactions from environments that already produced "high functioning," maybe "thinking," and perhaps even sentient WDNNs in the form of the human brain is likely to leap-frog such nascent nets into a complexity similar to their creators at a greatly compressed speed.
Which is to say, human brains, after 4 billion years of selective evolution created virtual environments ( video games) that stimulate themselves in the way theyve been evolved to enjoy. It seems only reasonable that a similar styled net would tend to create recognizabe pattens of interaction to said environments.
And with similar results to thier cognition, too.

comments.author: @x3haloed
comments.text:
Seems to me that training an AI on Minecraft from the get-go is the wrong way to do it. As Jim Fan points out, Minecraft is open-ended without strong goals, which makes it a highly creative game. I think creativity is a self-satisfying and/or socially-satisfying endeavor. I think training a model on Minecraft without it first developing a sense of satisfaction or social satisfaction is missing the point, and therefore, the model will be trained either to meet a bunch of superficial goals designed by humans or it will be trained to please humans directly rather than pleasing itself.

I think, therefore, that training on open-ended creative endeavors is something that needs to happen after a model is complex enough to reward itself.
